Because "decryption" is the process or reversing encryption, to find exactly the original input. One-way hash functions are, as the name suggests, one way. They can't be reversed because there are an infinite number of other inputs that can hash to the same value as the original password does. To gain access you only need 1 of these inputs, not necessarily the original password. However, most users choose shitty passwords with no entropy and so a dictionary attack can often find common words that people use and be reasonably sure that, if it works, it is actually the original password. But never 100% sure.

They can't be reversed because there are an infinite number of other inputs that can hash to the same value as the original password does.

This would seem like it would make it easier to reverse.

The essential thing though is hashes are designed to be one way if they are working right whereas encryption is designed to be decrypted. Is that right?

This would seem like it would make it easier to reverse.

It makes it impossible to reverse by brute force, because if you find an input that hashes to the desired value, it's just one of many such inputs (of which the original password is just one).

Gaining access to someone's account by finding a hash collision isn't the same thing as "reversing". Reversing would mean finding the users exact, original password (which they may have reused on 20 other accounts). That's a critical point because every website will use a different hashing routine, so finding a collision for one site doesn't lead to gaining access on every other site where the user reused the same password, whereas finding the original password would.

If people implement password hashing properly, it's also cost prohibitive to even find a single collision (requiring millions of dollars worth of CPU time).
There is a good chance you can find the original input therefor "decrypting", but also a good chance you can find a hash collision using another input which will work just as well, at least with md5.

There is a good chance you can find the original input

There's a good chance you can find an input that hashes to the same value via a dictionary attack -- but even a string that appears in a dictionary and collides with the hash value doesn't make it a dead certainty that it's the users actual, original password. It just makes it overwhelmingly likely. Encryption is reversible by definition, whereas hashing is not reversible by definition.
